brand-q3.answer: A display face for brand moments, with a sans for text
brand-q3.why: Bricolage Grotesque for display and headings, DM Sans for text: loud where the brand speaks, easy where people read.

items.label: Readability
items.text: Body text sits in DM Sans, a low-contrast sans that reads easily in short copy.

items.label: Legibility
items.text: DM Sans keeps simple, open shapes at small sizes; the display face never sets small text.

items.label: Scalability
items.text: Both are variable: Bricolage Grotesque has optical size, width and weight axes, and DM Sans optical size and weight.

items.label: Numerals
items.text: Numbers are few and set in DM Sans, in short copy rather than tables.

items.label: Scripts and languages
items.text: Latin, with accents; other scripts need faces chosen for the same voice.

items.label: Recognition
items.text: Bricolage Grotesque's character is the brand's: people know it by its headlines.

items.label: Familiarity
items.text: DM Sans for text keeps reading familiar while the display face takes the risks.

items.label: Personality
items.text: Bold and confident, as the brand answer asks.

items.label: Performance
items.text: Two variable families, one file each.

items.label: Licensing
items.text: SIL Open Font License, both: free to embed in apps and on the web.

items.label: Fallback and pairing
items.text: Falls back to system-ui, as its tokens say; DM Sans is the display face's text pair.

For hover and press feedback, use motion.duration.feedback (fast). Don't use an instant change. Fast feedback, on the brand's spring. An instant change drops the brand's motion.

items.text: Iconography · How many icon sizes exist? → Two
For an icon with no label, use not used: always add a word. Don't use an icon button with a hover hint. On phones, hover hints never show; a word says what will happen.
For an action on one row or item, use button ghost with a word. Don't use an icon alone. Visitors come rarely, so they never learn an icon. A word says what will happen.
Button's ghost variant. The alternative next to the primary, and row actions with a word.
Button's icon size isn't used. Phones first: hover hints never show, so every button has a word.
Empty's icon variant. A two-tone icon in a tile, for a small region where a picture would push the words away.
Input group's inline-start align. The search icon before the text.

accessibility-values.why: Visitors come from social posts on phones.
because: Where do people use it? → On the move

items.text: Accessibility · Which states get their own visible value? → Those and pressed
For an icon with no label, use not used: always add a word. Don't use an icon button with a hover hint. On phones, hover hints never show; a word says what will happen.
For the smallest clickable thing, use size.control.default (touch). Don't use a compact control. Most visitors arrive on phones, and a compact control is too small for a thumb.
Button's default size. Every button, at touch size: phones first.
Button's compact size isn't used. Phones first: no compact controls.
Button's icon size isn't used. Phones first: hover hints never show, so every button has a word.
Field's horizontal orientation isn't used. Phones first: there is no room beside the field.
Input group's inline-end align. The unit after the value, or the clear button with a word: hover hints never show on phones.
Item's default size. Every row, at touch size: phones first.
Item's sm size isn't used. Phones first: no compact rows.
Toggle's default size. Every toggle, at touch size: phones first.
Toggle's sm size isn't used. Phones first: no compact controls.

items.text: For a value with no token, use the closest semantic token, then ask for a new one. Don't use a raw value in the component. The next campaign changes primitives; raw values would stay behind.

because: What does the product do for the business? → Sells and converts

voice-count.why: Playful in headlines, plain in errors.
because: What is a costly mistake? → Looking off-brand

items.text: For the words of an error, use plain first, a light touch after. Don't use a joke before the fix. Playful copy must never hide what went wrong.
For a confirmation question, use Plain. No jokes when something is lost. Don't use playful copy. Loss is never the moment for a joke.
Badge's danger tone isn't used. Nothing on a launch page is labeled as failed; errors are plain sentences.
Toast's neutral tone. A light note that something changed.
Toast's danger tone. Plain first, a light touch after: That didn't go through.
Alert's default variant isn't used. Alerts here only report a sign-up that did not go through; confirmations go in a toast.
Alert's destructive variant. A sign-up that did not go through: plain first, then how to recover, with a word beside the color.

voice-definition.why: Principles and examples guide each campaign's writers.
because: Who maintains the system? → An agency
What should the brand feel like? → Bold
How visible is the brand in the interface? → Loud

items.text: For a paragraph or help text, use type.body, short. Don't use long paragraphs. Short copy keeps the energy.
For a button label, use a short verb that moves: Join, Try, Go. Don't use "Learn more". Big moments need verbs with energy.
For a success message, use celebrate, briefly. Don't use a long thank-you. A short celebration is remembered.
For an empty state, use playful, with a clear next step. Don't use a dead end. Playful words still need a way forward.
For a first visit, use one bold line and one button. Don't use a paragraph of copy. Visitors from a social post give a few seconds.
Toast's success tone. Celebrate, briefly: You're on the list. See you at launch.
